scenes.title: Which way from S to E is cheapest?
scenes.narration: Say you want the cheapest way to get from S to E.

steps.say: Each arrow is a one way road, and its number is what that road costs.
S is where we start, and E is where we want to end up.
One way is S to A, then A to E. That costs four plus six, which is ten.
Another is S to B, B to C, then C to E. That costs two plus five plus one, which is eight.
Checking every route works on five places. On a real road map with millions of crossings, there are far too many routes to try.
Dijkstra's method keeps a table instead.
For each place it notes the cheapest cost found so far, the place you came from, and whether that cost is settled.

scenes.title: Visit the cheapest place first
scenes.narration: First, write a starting guess for every place.

steps.say: S starts at zero, since it costs nothing to stay put.
Every other place starts at infinity, because we have no route to it yet.
S is the smallest, so we visit it first, and its zero is final.
From S, the road to A costs four. So A drops from infinity to four, and we note that it came from S.
The road to B costs two. So B is two, also from S.
Now the greedy rule. Of the places not yet visited, pick the one with the smallest cost.
That is B, at two. No road costs less than nothing, so no other way can reach B for less.

scenes.title: A detour through B is cheaper
scenes.narration: Now we look at the roads leaving B.

steps.say: We already know a way to A that costs four, straight from S.
But going S to B, then B to A, costs two plus one, which is three. Three is less than four.
So we cross out four, write three, and note that A now comes from B.
This is called relaxing a road. We found a shortcut, so we replace the old guess.
The road from B to C costs five, so C becomes seven, by way of B.

scenes.title: Repeat until E is settled
scenes.narration: We keep repeating the same two moves: pick the cheapest unvisited place, then relax the roads leaving it.

steps.say: A is cheapest at three, so we visit it.
Through A, C costs three plus two, which is five. That beats seven.
And E costs three plus six, which is nine.
C is next, at five.
Through C, E costs five plus one, which is six. Six beats nine.
Now E is the cheapest place left, so its cost of six is settled, and we can stop.
To read the route, follow the from column backward. E came from C, C from A, A from B, and B from S.
Turn that around, and the cheapest route is S, B, A, C, E, for a total of six.
